options.text: The electricity that powers a computer
Instructions written in a programming language that humans can read
The physical chips inside the computer
Data stored in a database

explanation_after: Source code is human-readable instructions. The computer cannot run it directly — it must be either compiled (translated all at once into machine code) or interpreted (translated line-by-line as it runs). Python is interpreted, which is one reason it feels fast to write but runs slower than compiled languages.

stem: Code executes in what order by default?

options.text: Bottom to top
Randomly — whichever line seems most important
Top to bottom, left to right
Alphabetically by variable name

explanation_after: Code runs top to bottom unless something explicitly changes the order — like a loop (repeats), a function call (jumps to another block), or a conditional (skips lines). Understanding this default order is foundational to reading any program.

stem: Why do AI systems still need code even if they 'learn' from data?

options.text: They don't — AI systems write themselves
Code defines the structure, training loop, and rules of what the AI is allowed to do
Code is only needed to connect AI to the internet
Code is only needed for older AI systems

explanation_after: An AI model learns WHAT to do from data, but the CODE defines HOW it learns — the architecture, training loop, loss function, data pipeline, and deployment. Even GPT-4 is thousands of lines of code wrapped around a trained model. Learning AI engineering means understanding both the code structure and the learning process.

stem: What is the key difference between a compiled language and an interpreted language?

options.text: Compiled languages are translated entirely into machine code before running; interpreted languages are translated and executed line-by-line as the program runs
Compiled languages don't need to be translated into machine code at all
Interpreted languages always run faster than compiled languages
There is no real difference between the two approaches

explanation_after: A compiler translates the whole program into machine code up front, producing a standalone executable. An interpreter reads and executes the source code line-by-line each time the program runs, with no separate compilation step. Python is interpreted (technically compiled to bytecode then interpreted), which is part of why it's quick to write and test but generally slower than compiled languages like C++.

stem:
What is the order of output for this code?

print('A')
print('B')
print('C')

options.text: C, B, A
A, B, C
B, A, C
All three print at exactly the same time

explanation_after: With no loops, functions, or conditionals to redirect execution, Python simply runs each line in the order it appears: top to bottom. Line 1 runs, then line 2, then line 3 — producing A, B, C in that order.

stem: A trained model produces wrong predictions. Where is the underlying bug most likely to be found?

options.text: Bugs can only exist in the training data, never in code
In the code itself — such as how data is loaded, preprocessed, or how the training loop is written — since a wrong prediction can stem from any step in that code path, not just the learned parameters
In the electricity supplying the computer
AI models cannot have bugs, only humans can have bugs

explanation_after: A trained model's behavior is the product of executing code, start to finish: data loading code, preprocessing code, the training loop, and the inference code that generates predictions. Reading code carefully and understanding its execution order — the exact skill this question tests — is essential to finding where a bug entered, because 'the model is wrong' could mean the label column was shuffled, the loss was computed incorrectly, or a dozen other code-level issues.
